content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published recommendations on antenatal care (ANC) to ensure a positive pregnancy experience. These guidelines are designed to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes through evidence-based interventions. Below are the key points and considerations outlined in the document: 1. Nutritional Interventions: For pregnant women, dietary and/or exercise interventions compared to standard ANC may improve maternal and perinatal outcomes, including reducing maternal morbidity (e.g., excessive weight gain, anemia, gestational diabetes mellitus), improving delivery outcomes, and enhancing maternal satisfaction. In undernourished populations, energy and protein dietary education or supplementation compared to no intervention may improve maternal and perinatal outcomes, such as reducing low birth weight, preterm birth, and neonatal mortality. 2. Iron Supplementation: Daily iron supplementation, with or without folic acid, compared to no supplementation or placebo, may reduce maternal anemia, infections, and improve maternal satisfaction. It may also reduce fetal and newborn morbidity (e.g., congenital anomalies, low birth weight, preterm birth) and mortality. 3. Maternal Assessment: Accurate detection of anemia (hemoglobin <11 g/dL or <10 g/dL) and severe anemia (<6 g/dL) is critical. Screening for asymptomatic urinary tract infections (≥10⁵ CFU/mL of a single pathogen) is recommended to prevent complications. Maternal satisfaction with care is a priority outcome. 4. Preventive Measures: For pregnant women with asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB), a course of antibiotics compared to no antibiotics may reduce maternal infections, improve satisfaction, and decrease fetal and newborn morbidity (e.g., low birth weight, preterm birth) and mortality. 5. Interventions for Common Pregnancy Symptoms: For nausea and vomiting, pharmacological or non-pharmacological interventions compared to no treatment may provide symptomatic relief, improve maternal satisfaction, and reduce side effects. For heartburn, similar interventions may alleviate symptoms and improve maternal satisfaction. For leg cramps, interventions may reduce morbidity and improve outcomes. For pelvic and back pain, interventions may provide symptomatic relief and improve maternal satisfaction. For constipation, interventions may alleviate symptoms and enhance maternal satisfaction. For varicose veins and edema, interventions may provide symptomatic relief and improve maternal satisfaction. 6. Health System Interventions: Encouraging pregnant women to carry their own ANC case notes may improve the quality of care and maternal satisfaction. Optimizing health worker roles through task shifting can improve access to key maternal and newborn health interventions, especially in remote and rural areas. 7. Screening and Management of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM): Strategies for screening and managing GDM were identified as requiring further in-depth consideration. WHO plans to develop specific guidelines on GDM in collaboration with diabetes experts. 8. Fetal Assessment: Interventions such as reactive cardiotocography and detection of multiple pregnancies are recommended to improve maternal satisfaction and reduce fetal and newborn morbidity and mortality. 9. Guidelines on Substance Use and Tobacco Exposure: WHO provides recommendations for the prevention and management of tobacco use and second-hand smoke exposure during pregnancy, as well as guidelines for managing substance use disorders in pregnancy. 10. HIV and Syphilis Testing: Consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services and syphilis detection tests are included to improve maternal and fetal outcomes. 11. Malaria Treatment: WHO has published guidelines for the treatment of malaria during pregnancy to reduce maternal and fetal complications. 12. Considerations for Evidence and Bias: Some questions, such as the prognostic value of GDM detection tests and vibracoustic stimulation, were omitted due to insufficient evidence synthesis within the timeframe. However, these omissions were not considered to bias the guidelines. 13. Future Directions: WHO plans to develop specific guidelines on GDM and other areas requiring further evidence synthesis, in collaboration with relevant experts and departments. These recommendations aim to provide comprehensive, evidence-based guidance to improve maternal and perinatal health outcomes, ensuring a positive pregnancy experience for women worldwide.
